item.title: New Research Reveals How Long Stays in Space Affects the Human Genome
item.description: A new study in Science Advances addresses the pressing questions about how long-duration exposure to microgravity affects the human genome.

item.title: Plants shift gene activity within minutes of entering spaceflight, experiment reveals
item.description: Plants begin responding to spaceflight almost immediately after leaving Earth, according to a new University of Florida study that captured the earliest stages of biological adaptation during a commercial suborbital mission. Published in the journal npj Microgravity, the study reports the results of an experiment conducted by a UF astronaut during Blue Origin's New Shepard NS-26 flight on Aug. 29, 2024.

item.title: How lessons from fisheries management could help us govern Earth's orbital space
item.description: The space industry is rapidly expanding. About 20,000 satellites already circle Earth, a number that could reach 100,000 by 2030. They bring growing environmental costs: space debris, collision risks, atmospheric pollution from launches and reentry and interference with astronomical observations.

item.title: Two large asteroids found spinning as fast as a fairground ride
item.description: Rocks in the asteroid belt rotating at ultra-fast speeds suggest our understanding of asteroid structure might be wrong

item.title: Enigmatic Mercury will remain a puzzle until someone sends a lander
item.description: Mercury remains one of our solar system's most elusive and difficult planets to study. It's easier to send probes to the icy moons of Saturn or Jupiter, or even to Pluto, than to land on our innermost planet, Mercury.

item.title: Retired pilot helps historical society buy Neil Armstrong's boyhood home for tours
item.description: Ken Schreiber was 9 when Neil Armstrong took his first steps on the moon in 1969—a moment he would never forget. Like Armstrong, he became a military fighter pilot.

item.title: Why the Drake equation is still important 65 years after its creation
item.description: The Drake equation provides a way to guess how many aliens we might be able to communicate with, but it’s also a prime example of the importance of scientific guessing, says columnist Leah Crane

item.title: Salt crystals could hold clues to life beneath Enceladus's ice
item.description: The ocean beneath Saturn's moon Enceladus lies under kilometers of ice, but some of its contents do reach the surface. Jets near the south pole spray out water vapor and icy particles, offering a way to investigate the hidden ocean without drilling down to it.

item.title: Oct. 17, 1956: Birth of Mae Jemison
item.description: Born Oct. 17, 1956, in Decatur, Alabama, and raised in Chicago, Mae Jemison showed a passion and talent for science from early in her childhood. After graduating high school by the age of 16, Jemison attended Stanford University and earned a B.S. in chemical engineering and a B.A. in African American studies. item.title: NASA's Hubble spies spiral's edge
item.description: This NASA Hubble Space Telescope image features the edge-on, intermediate spiral galaxy NGC 1827, located roughly 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, the Dove. Hubble captured the image as part of a survey looking at 260 satellite galaxies around 22 Milky Way–like host galaxies within a radius of about 32 million light-years from Earth. item.title: Forecasting air drag with deep learning helps predict when uncontrolled satellites and rocket stages fall to Earth
item.description: On May 10, 2025, a spacecraft built in the Soviet Union to land on Venus came home. Launched in 1972, Cosmos-482 was stranded by a failed upper stage of its rocket and circled Earth for 53 years. In its last days, several space agencies and research groups forecasted when it would fall, and therefore where. Roscosmos later reported that it came down in the Indian Ocean, west of Jakarta.

item.title: In the Search for Exoplanets, Some Failures Are A Success
item.description: Astronomers used decades of archival data and new radial velocity measurements to search for exoplanets around a neaby binary star, 70 Oph AB. They didn't find any, which can seem like a failure. But in this case, their work only ruled out large, Jupiter-mass planets at certain distances. There could still be Earth-sized planets there, and their precise findings will only fuel a deeper search with more powerful telescopes.

item.title: The Flavor of Neutrinos Could Determine How a Large Star Dies
item.description: Neutrinos come in three different flavors. A new study finds that neutrino flavor could play a significant role in whether a dying star becomes a supernova or collapses directly into a black hole.

item.title: A Radio Phoenix Beyond the Zone of Avoidance
item.description: Years ago, astronomers spotted a strange radio formation beyond the Zone of Avoidance. The formation resembles a treble clef, a symbol in musical notation, and the nickname has stuck. Determining what created it has been difficult, but new research has revealed that the Treble Clef is a radio phoenix.

item.title: The next generation’s guide to the new space economy
item.description: An industry report published by students in an MIT aerospace entrepreneurship class lays out guidance for aspiring space leaders and investors.

item.title: A lack of rockets is creating a crisis for space technology companies
item.description: SpaceX’s changing priorities, the war in Ukraine and a lack of competitors are all causing a launch crisis that might last years

item.title: Orionid, Taurid Meteors Haunt October Skies
item.description: Fall meteor season has begun. Late October not only sees dusk falling ever earlier as ghouls and goblins walk the Earth on Halloween, but it also sees the peak of two fine annual meteor showers kicking off Halloween season: the Orionid and Taurid meteor showers.

item.title: Chandrasekhar Placed A Limit On White Dwarfs, But A New Study Finds This Limit Is Not Absolute
item.description: The Chandrasekhar limit states that a white dwarf can be no larger than 1.4 solar masses. A new study demonstrates how highly magnetized white dwarfs could overcome that limit, and how such super-Chandrasekhar white dwarfs could form.

item.title: Hypernovae May Be All Hype, No Nova
item.description: Astrophysicists think that hypernovae are the most powerful stellar explosions in the Universe. They're the most explosive type of core-collapse supernova. But the evidence for them is not voluminous, and new research pokes holes in it, pointing out that hypernovae may not actually exist.

item.title: A Red Dwarf is Taking its Time Eating a Brown Dwarf
item.description: Astronomers detected an unusual triangular light curve about 300 light years away. They were searching for Black Widow Binaries, where a dense neutron star eats its companion. But they found something different: an M dwarf slowly eating its binary companion brown dwarf.

item.title: SpaceX’s Starship will orbit Earth for first time during next flight
item.description: Starship's next test flight will be its first orbital mission. The craft will also release working Starlink V3 satellites for the first time, making the flight the first commercially useful Starship mission

item.title: Scientists Detect Rare Type of Wood Alcohol in Space
item.description: As part of the ALMA COMPASS Large program, an international research team has detected a rare form of methanol in space for the first time.

item.title: Margaret Hamilton, computing pioneer who led software development for the Apollo program, dies at 90
item.description: Over two decades at MIT, Hamilton forged new paths in computer science and engineering. Her groundbreaking work included leading the team that programmed the first computers that took humans to the moon.

item.title: Supporting mission-driven space innovation, for Earth and beyond
item.description: Aurelia Institute, founded by a team from MIT, serves as a research lab, an education and outreach center, and a policy hub for the space industry.

item.title: Why gatekeeping is needed in the age of AI
item.description: Large language models have unleashed a torrent of text – dealing with it won't be easy
